title: Long-term limits on maximum ice sheet thickness around central Antarctic Peninsula nunataks
abstract: Understanding past ice sheet sensitivity to long-term climate cycles is essential to predict future sea-level rise. The Antarctic Peninsula Ice Sheet (APIS) is changing rapidly in one of Antarctica’s fastest warming regions. However, APIS thickness changes are poorly understood because there are limited terrestrial records of deglaciation. Here, the gap is filled by measuring cosmogenic nuclide ( 10 Be, 26 Al and 21 Ne) concentrations in 34 bedrock and boulder samples from high elevation nunataks in the APIS interior. Samples near the current ice surface record repeated burial by non-erosive ice mostly since ~890 ka. Nuclide ratios indicate that surfaces more than 121 – 170 m above current ice levels at Mount Faith, Mount Sullivan, and Engel Peaks have been ice-free for millions of years, reaching production-decay-erosion equilibrium with erosion rates as low as 0.14 ± 0.02 m Myr -1 . These limits contrast with numerical models which predict >250 m of thinning since the last glacial maximum, suggesting they are overestimating sea-level contribution from the central and eastern Antarctic Peninsula.

title: The balance of evidence indicates a slowing AMOC
abstract: arXiv:2611.23429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a critical component of the climate system. Climate models have long predicted a slowing of the AMOC due to anthropogenic forcing, with a risk of passing tipping points in the future. The question of whether the AMOC is already weakening is still somewhat controversial. Continuous monitoring is only available for the past two decades, a period too short to tease apart contributions of natural variability and climate change. Reconstructions of AMOC strength going back further in time have different limitations which are debated in the literature. Here we compile and discuss this heterogeneous body of evidence, focusing on latitudes south of 45{\deg}N where northward and southward flow are separated vertically. We conclude that the balance of multiple lines of evidence strongly supports a past and ongoing AMOC slowing in response to global warming, although some uncertainty remains regarding its magnitude and timing.

title: Basal sliding and ice rheology in West Antarctica constrained by multi-epoch satellite observations
abstract: A new method for the calibration of uncertain parameters in large-scale viscous ice-flow models is presented, with particular focus on the basal sliding law and ice rheology.The approach combines Bayesian inference with the rich information contained in successive satellite observations of ice-sheet elevation and velocity changes, and does not require knowledge of the surface or basal mass balance.The method is validated on a synthetic glacier with known physics, and subsequently applied to West Antarctica.The results support earlier evidence for a plastic basal rheology and strongly non-Newtonian creep within the regions ice streams.The stochastic framework provides a robust foundation for improved predictive simulations, offering data-driven constraints on how basal sliding and ice rheology may influence West Antarcticas future contribution to sea-level rise.

title: Twenty Years of data from the RAPID-MOCHA-WBTS array: Long-Term Changes in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, Heat and Freshwater Transports
abstract: Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) For over 20 years, measurements across the Atlantic at 26° N has continuously recorded the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation that carry heat northward and help shape the climate. This paper describes the resulting data, how they are produced and shared, and how they show changes in these ocean circulation over time. It also releases the computer code used to produce them, so anyone can reproduce and reuse the data.

title: Greenland ice sheet retreat intensifies the African monsoon through a polar-tropical atmospheric teleconnection
abstract: Global climate forcing drives major changes in the North African summer monsoon (NASM), yet how high-latitude cryospheric changes influence tropical hydroclimate through atmospheric dynamics remains unclear. Integrating paleoclimate proxy evidence with coupled climate-model simulations, sensitivity experiments, and idealized atmospheric modeling, we show that Greenland Ice Sheet (GrIS) retreat acts as a dynamically important amplifier of NASM rainfall. Using the mid-Pliocene as a natural experiment for sustained global warming, we find that NASM rainfall was markedly stronger than that simulated under transient future warming for comparable global-mean temperature increases. GrIS retreat enhances Arctic warming, thereby perturbing the upper-tropospheric westerly jet and triggering a stationary Rossby wave train linking Greenland to North Africa. This polar–tropical atmospheric teleconnection strengthens monsoon circulation and moisture convergence, producing wetter conditions across the Sahara–Sahel. These results reveal a high-latitude pathway through which slow cryospheric changes modulate low-latitude monsoon variability under sustained warming.

title: Cyclical high-magnitude lake drainage slows Greenland ice sheet motion
abstract: Global glacier recession is driving a rapid increase in the number and volume of ice-marginal lakes, leading to more frequent Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs). The long-term impact of GLOFs on glacier dynamics remains poorly understood, including in Greenland, which holds the largest glacial lake volume in the world. Here, using multi-decadal observations from Isortuarsuup Sermia, Southwest Greenland, we reveal that cyclical GLOFs regulate ice sheet motion. We identify a ‘sawtooth’ pattern of ice-dynamics, whereby multi-year acceleration is terminated abruptly by high-magnitude lake-drainage that resets the glacier to a ‘quiescent’ state for several years. The 2022 event exemplifies this process: the near-terminus ice velocity accelerated briefly from a pre-event baseline of ~200 m a −1 to ~1000 m a −1 before dropping to ~50 m a −1 over subsequent years. Each GLOF releases an immense meltwater volume (mean discharge in 2022 ~17000 m³ s −1), carving a ~1.5-km-wide, efficient subglacial channel. This channel enables extensive lowering of the subglacial water pressure, increasing ice–bed friction and suppressing ice motion. As climate warming increases GLOF frequency, this powerful negative feedback will modulate ice sheet motion acting as a brake on ice-dynamics at the margins of the Greenland Ice Sheet.

title: Characterizing ENSO Teleconnections Impact on Gross Primary Productivity across CMIP6 Earth System Models
abstract: Abstract The El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the dominant mode of interannual variability in the climate system, altering global circulation patterns and causing changes in temperature and precipitation in remote regions through teleconnections. Because ecosystems are sensitive to climate variations, ENSO teleconnections have large implications for the magnitude of carbon uptake by terrestrial vegetation at interannual timescales. Using ten CMIP6 Earth System Models during 1950–2014, we find global carbon uptake is reduced 0.68± 0.18 PgC per °C increase in the Nino3.4 sea surface temperature, primarily due to reduced gross primary productivity (GPP), with a secondary contribution from increased heterotrophic respiration. We quantify the ENSO impact on GPP and identify several key regions in the tropics (Amazon, Southeast Asia) and extratropics (Australia, Northwest North America) where the ensemble shows regionally coherent, statistically significant changes to GPP. In the Amazon, most models suppress GPP due to increased temperature, but three models exhibit a weaker reduction or slight enhancement in GPP. Inter-model differences in background soil moisture state mediate the relative importance of temperature compared to radiation in controlling total and ENSO-driven GPP variability in the Amazon, with drier models exhibiting a stronger temperature-driven response and tending to exhibit greater reductions in GPP associated with ENSO. Our results suggest that, across the ensemble, land model sensitivities to simulated physical climate anomalies play a large role in the GPP response to ENSO conditions and that these responses differ regionally even within the same latitude range.

title: A multi-decadal dataset of surface damage  on Antarctic ice shelves (1999–2024)
abstract: Many Antarctic ice shelves are thinning and retreating, threatening future sea-level rise. Surface damage indicates structural weakening, but long-term records are scarce. We created a multi-decadal surface damage record for nine representative Antarctic ice shelves using satellite imagery and deep learning. Among them, Pine Island, Thwaites and Scar Inlet have experienced the most significant changes in surface damage during the study period, providing insights into ice shelf stability.

title: West Antarctic ice retreat temporarily halted with transient rheology in future climate projections
abstract: Sea level change and ice sheet stability depend on how Earth’s bedrock warps as ice melts. Rock experiments show that traditional models for bedrock deformation leave out important processes relevant for modern ice loss. We simulate the coevolution of the Antarctic ice sheet and global sea level under various climate change scenarios. When more realistic bedrock behavior is considered, Antarctic ice retreat is delayed. Ultimately, this has implications for larger Earth system feedbacks.

title: Mountain carbon budgets miss cryosphere hazard events
abstract: Warming is destabilizing the mountain cryosphere and triggering more frequent hazard events. These hazards mobilize large stores of carbon as well as rock, ice and water. Yet mountain carbon budgets largely overlook this flux, because routine monitoring rarely operates at the time, location and resolution that hazard events demand. We argue that cryosphere hazards should be treated as carbon events and set out how to close the gap. Here, cryosphere hazard events are mass movements in glacial and permafrost terrain whose onset is abrupt relative to gradual degradation, together with the cascades they trigger (Ding et al., 2021;Zhang et al., 2025). They range from rock-ice avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) lasting hours to retrogressive thaw slumps that develop within days to years as a form of abrupt thaw (Turetsky et al., 2020).At high elevations, warming is often amplified (Pepin et al., 2015(Pepin et al., , 2025)). Global glacier mass-loss rates rose by 36 ± 10% between 2000-2011and 2012-2023(Zemp et al., 2025)), and mountain permafrost is warming (Wu and Zhang, 2008;Noetzli et al., 2024) and thawing abruptly (Turetsky et al., 2020). GLOF frequency in the Third Pole has risen since 1980 (Zhang et al., 2023), and global GLOFs from moraine-dammed lakes increased from 5.2 to 15.2 per year between 1981-1990and 2011-2020(Zhang et al., 2025)). Retrogressive thaw slumps are spreading rapidly in alpine permafrost (Xia et al., 2024), driving cascading damage locally and downstream (Ding et al., 2021;Shugar et al., 2021). Existing frameworks recognize erosion, lateral transport, and outgassing as carbon pathways (Chapin et al., 2006;Hilton and West, 2020;Regnier et al., 2022), but lack a way to quantify hazard-driven mobilization and trace its fate (Figure 1a).A complete net ecosystem carbon budget needs vertical exchange from eddy covariance and chambers, and lateral export and outgassing from river and lake sampling (Chapin et al., 2006;Keenan and Williams, 2018), yet these observations rarely capture brief events or hillslope-channel transport.Three monitoring problems limit how cryosphere hazards enter carbon budgets. Temporal aliasing means periodic monitoring misses an event when the sampling interval exceeds a hazard-driven concentration peak. Extrapolation error means that, once a hazard resets sediment and carbon availability, pre-event concentration-discharge relationships no longer predict post-event fluxes. Material selectivity means that sampling of dissolved and suspended loads excludes carbon moved as woody debris, coarse bedload, or buried in deposits. No single method can constrain these fluxes: atmospheric observations cannot resolve lateral transfers, and satellite erosion detection cannot quantify the concentration or reactivity of displaced material. Figure 1. (a) Conceptual diagram showing cryosphere hazards-induced mobilization, transport, and transformation of carbon along a hazard-to-fate cascade. Cryosphere hazards, including glacier detachment, rock-ice avalanche, glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) and thaw slump, connect mountain carbon stores to downstream environments. Cascading flows entrain carbon from soils, rock debris and vegetation, transporting it through channels to valley floors and receiving waters. Along these pathways, decomposition can release carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4), whereas deposition and burial can retain carbon and vegetation recovery can restore CO2 uptake. Subsequent remobilization can expose stored material to further transport and decomposition, extending carbon effects beyond the initial disturbance. Whether a disturbance increases or decreases net carbon transfer to the atmosphere depends on carbon fate and ecosystem uptake, evaluated against a no-event trajectory over the same area and period. The diagram presents a conceptual accounting framework, not a quantified carbon budget, and unquantified pathways should not be read as zero fluxes. Over an accounting period, stock change within the boundary is ΔCstock = -Fatm -Fexport (Eq. 1), where Fatm is the cumulative net carbon flux to the atmosphere and Fexport is the net lateral export across the boundary, both positive when carbon leaves the system; burial within the boundary redistributes carbon within ΔCstock. The event term is □□!"!#$ = ∑ [□□ %$&,!"!#$($) -□□ %$&,*!+($) ] $ ! $ "(Eq. 2), relative to a no-event trajectory; Eevent > 0 indicates a source. POC, particulate organic carbon; DOC, dissolved organic carbon; DIC, dissolved inorganic carbon. (b) Gaps in representing cryosphere hazard events in mountain carbon budgets and ways forward.The consequence is systematic omission rather than random error. Hazard-driven fluxes are rare, brief and often occur in inaccessible terrain, so the disturbance-transfer term in the net ecosystem carbon balance usually lacks an empirical estimate and is underestimated. Known hazard fluxes come almost entirely from bespoke post-event surveys; after a GLOF, channelarmour disruption exposed sediment invisible to pre-event rating curves (Cook et al., 2018).The magnitude missed varies, so no single correction factor works across events. Earthquakeand storm-triggered landslides, used here as process analogues because their carbon export has been measured, show this variability. Landslide pulses increased biospheric carbon export (Hilton et al., 2008;Wang et al., 2016) and accounted for roughly 40% of organic carbon export in two New Zealand catchments (Howarth et al., 2025), whereas the Gorkha earthquake produced no detectable perturbation (Märki et al., 2021). Atmospheric inversions constrain aggregate CO2 exchange without attributing sources (Ciais et al., 2022), so a hazard signal may already sit within them unresolved.Cryosphere hazard cascades mobilize carbon spanning orders of magnitude in age and lability, from millennial permafrost organic matter and petrogenic rock carbon to recently fixed vegetation (Figure 1a). Source areas above treeline hold little biomass, but downstream cascades cross carbon-rich soils and forests. The 2023 South Lhonak disaster released about 50 million m 3 of water and eroded about 270 million m 3 of sediment (Sattar et al., 2025), yet its carbon was not estimated. A simple calculation shows the scale at stake. Assume a dry bulk density of 1.3-1.8 t/m 3 (Ji et al., 2020) and an organic carbon content of 0.43-0.79% for landslide debris from the Tibetan Plateau (Wang et al., 2023). The ~91 million m 3 of debris (excluding ice) detached at the China-Nepal border in 2026 (Li et al., 2026) would then hold roughly 0.51-1.29 Tg of organic carbon. That gross lateral mobilization is about 2.5-6.5 times the annual biospheric organic carbon export of the much larger Narayani catchment (Märki et al., 2021, their Fig. 4), mobilized in a few hours. This ratio is an upper bound, because the debris carbon also includes petrogenic carbon. Whether this carbon is flushed downstream, buried, or oxidized in the valley, it falls outside budgets built on routine river sampling.Mobilization changes the conditions that regulate decomposition. Aggregate disruption and exposure can increase microbial access, whereas mineral association and rapid burial may protect organic matter (Hilton and West, 2020). Carbon age alone does not determine lability.Old yet bioavailable dissolved organic matter occurs in Alaskan glacial runoff (Hood et al., 2009), and old carbon contributes substantially to river CO2 emissions (Dean et al., 2025). At permafrost thaw slumps, vegetation-free surfaces reduced respiration by about one-half but gross primary productivity by about four-fifths (Jiang et al., 2026a), and a plateau-wide synthesis found lower respiration in collapsed areas but increased CH4 release in alpine swamp meadows (Jia et al., 2026). Floods bury soil and biomass in valley fills, lakes and reservoirs, while channel reworking can later expose them. Drained thermokarst and proglacial lake beds and debris-flow surfaces are a particular blind spot, because dry inland waters can still emit carbon (Keller et al., 2020). The fate of mobilized carbon depends jointly on transport speed and reaction kinetics. Rapid flushing through cold, sediment-rich channels can export carbon before substantial mineralization, whereas retention in oxygenated sediments prolongs microbial breakdown.Hazards also mobilize inorganic carbon, exposing reactive minerals and changing waterrock interactions (Hawkings et al., 2026). Carbonic acid weathering and carbonation can consume CO2 (Styllas et al., 2026), whereas sulfide oxidation coupled to carbonate dissolution can release it (Hilton and West, 2020), and oxidation of petrogenic organic carbon is another CO2 source (Zondervan et al., 2023). In Tibetan Plateau rivers, net weathering is estimated to offset about 35% of river CO2 emissions (Zhang et al., 2026). Because hazard events mix inorganic and organic carbon, assessments based only on organic carbon decomposition may miss part of the response (Middelburg, 2024). The same mobilization couples carbon with other element cycles: permafrost thaw can increase N2O emissions (Voigt et al., 2020), glacial erosion exports reactive phosphorus (Hawkings et al., 2016), and thaw slumps release permafrost mercury, sharply raising methylmercury concentrations downstream (Schuster et al., 2018;St. Pierre et al., 2018).Whether a hazard event is a carbon source or sink depends on the quantity, boundary and processes assessed. Gross mobilization is the displacement of carbon from its original location, outlet export its transfer across a defined boundary, and net atmospheric exchange its transfer to or from the atmosphere. Redeposition within the same boundary redistributes carbon without creating a landscape sink, so these quantities should be accounted for separately and reconciled through mass balance (Eq. 1, Figure 1). We define the event term (Eq. 2, Figure 1) as cumulative net atmospheric carbon exchange with the event minus that under a specified no-event trajectory. Positive values indicate additional release or reduced uptake (a source), and negative values indicate additional uptake or avoided release (a sink). The reference site should share the affected site's warming and hydrology, differing only in the absence of the hazard. An event can thus increase atmospheric carbon relative to this reference while the landscape remains a net sink. Burial and ecological recovery can offset part of the disturbance, although forested-landslide evidence should be applied cautiously to alpine terrain. Post-Wenchuan sediment storage and revegetation raised carbon mass by about 10% (Liu et al., 2026), whereas greenness recovery after tundra thaw slumps took a decade at low-Arctic sites and more than 30 years at high-Arctic and highelevation sites (Xia et al., 2026). Greenness recovery does not imply recovered soil carbon stocks or net ecosystem exchange, so persistent productivity losses may matter even when deposited organic matter decomposes slowly.The atmospheric benefit of burial also depends on the reference trajectory. Relocating organic matter that would otherwise have remained protected adds little, whereas preserving material that would otherwise decompose avoids emissions (Galy et al., 2007). Only regrowth exceeding the no-event trajectory lowers the event term, and preserving petrogenic organic carbon averts a geological release without removing fixed atmospheric carbon. These distinctions keep sediment accumulation from supporting unwarranted sequestration claims.Field observations constrain exchange at some thaw slumps, geomorphic reconstructions constrain mobilization pathways, and downstream studies constrain delayed transport, yet few link all three within one event. Assessments should also report CO2-C and CH4-C separately, and converting CH4 emissions into a forcing metric requires an explicit metric and time horizon.We propose four priorities to close this gap (Figure 1b). First, establish a common accounting basis. Each assessment should specify its spatial boundary, accounting period, carbon forms and disturbance coverage, carry unsampled intervals into the uncertainty (Chapin et al., 2006;Ciais et al., 2022), and report mobilization, boundary export and the event term separately (Figure 1, Eqs. 1-2). This separates fluxes missing from an assessment from disturbance effects included but not attributed. Shared event identifiers should connect hazard inventories, water samples, deposit surveys and gas-flux records, distinguishing new erosion from remobilization of previously surveyed material (Jiang et al., 2026b).Second, trace carbon from source areas through transport pathways to deposits. Converting eroded volumes into carbon mass requires source material measurements that capture differences among lithologies, soil horizons, particle sizes and woody debris, with uncertainty in ice content and dry density propagated. Provenance measurements should distinguish biospheric from petrogenic carbon, because depleted radiocarbon alone cannot separate the two, and water chemistry should constrain weathering pathways and their CO2 uptake or release (Hilton and West, 2020). Post-event deposits record retained material but cannot reconstruct the dissolved and fine particulate carbon exported during the event (Märki et al., 2021).Third, connect short-lived transport pulses to longer-term carbon effects. Pre-positioned automatic samplers and redundant stream sensors can capture flood dynamics where deployment is safe (Cook et al., 2018). Later observations should track channel deposits, exposed lake beds, soil gas exchange and vegetation through successive seasons (Keller et al., 2020;Xia et al., 2026). Paired disturbed and reference sites separate event effects from regional change, and sediment cores can extend instrumental records if chronology and postdepositional carbon loss are treated explicitly (Howarth et al., 2025).Fourth, represent event diversity and overlapping legacies in regional models. Multiplying event frequency by a single mean carbon yield obscures differences among carbon-poor headwaters, vegetated valleys and efficient depositional traps. Models should link mobilization to carbon provenance, connectivity, transformation and ecological recovery, while allowing event recurrence to change and later floods to remobilize earlier deposits. Comparison with independent outlet fluxes or stock changes over a common period can show whether explicit event representation improves budget estimates.The approach generates testable expectations. Events crossing carbon-rich terrain with direct channel connections should mobilize more biospheric carbon than events confined to mineral debris (Hilton and West, 2020). Stable deposits should retain carbon longer than frequently reworked channels, and slow revegetation should prolong reductions in uptake.Testing these expectations would show where event accounting changes the inferred mountain carbon balance. Cryosphere hazards are becoming more frequent as warming continues (Ding et al., 2021;Zhang et al., 2025;Jiang et al., 2026b;Richter, 2026), so the carbon they mobilize is a growing budget term, and closing the observational gap is necessary to determine its climate feedback.

title: Progress in high-resolution paleoclimatic and paleoenvironmental reconstructions at two Upper Pleistocene key localities in the loess type region of the Upper and Middle Rhine area (Germany)
abstract: In 1823/24 the term loess was introduced by Karl Caesar von Leonhard and its 200th anniversary was celebrated during the 2024 Loess Fest-conference in Mainz, Germany. Over these 200 years, loess research has evolved into a discipline of its own with initial approaches discussing the genesis and formation of this specific type of sediment, while later, the linkage to Quaternary climatic cycles was recognized. Nowadays, it is well known that loess–paleosol sequences (LPS) represent highly complex paleoclimatic and paleoenvironmental archives with great spatial extent in the terrestrial realm covering the entire Quaternary. Here we present the state of research for two LPS in von Leonhard’s eponym region that evolved to key sections for the last interglacial–glacial cycle during the last decades: Schwalbenberg in the Middle Rhine valley and Nussloch in the Upper Rhine area. We demonstrate that these sites contribute to a better understanding of the mechanisms controlling the interplay of sediment accumulation, soil formation, sediment relocation, and associated preservation of climate signals in LPS. Furthermore, methodological advances allow for reconstruction of paleoenvironmental and paleoclimatic changes throughout the Upper Pleistocene on millennial- to centennial-scale resolution, highlighting the sensitivity of western European LPS to northern hemispheric climate oscillations.

title: Proglacial lakes substantially modulate the surface mass balance of deglacial ice sheets
abstract: Towards the end of the last ice age large proglacial lakes formed at the margins of the retreating ice sheets, potentially staying cold due to the influence of melting ice. Modeling shows these lakes lowered summer air temperatures, increased snowfall, and in total reduced surface melt by 18 %–27 % for nearby ice sheets. If lakes stayed below 4 °C, melt dropped by 23 %–35 %, providing a substantial negative feedback for retreating of ice sheets.

title: Long‐Term Surface Meltwater Variability and Surface Fracture Patterns on the Amery Ice Shelf
journal: New Zealand Journal of Geology and Geophysics
abstract: Antarctic ice shelves buttress grounded ice, but surface meltwater can promote fracture opening when it enters pre‐existing crevasses. Although meltwater variability, water depth and fracture features have been examined separately on the Amery Ice Shelf, their spatial correspondence has received less attention. We integrated January meltwater maps for 2005–2026 with depth and volume estimates for melt seasons ending in 2014–2026 within a common spatial framework. Fracture inputs comprised published creavasse extraction maps for 2009 and 2014 and a Landsat‐derived map for 2025. Multi‐year melt water and creavess coupling indices described relative spatial co‐location. Seasonal indices combined water proximity, local fracture context and retrieved depth. Estimated seasonal volume peaked at 0.76 km 3 in 2017 and 0.75 km 3 in 2019. The 2025 volume was 0.44 km 3 , with generally smaller retrieved depths than in 2014 and 2017. January mapped meltwater area ranged from 26.2 km 2 in 2021 to 1178.1 km 2 in 2005 and reached 1058.4 km 2 in 2025. Recurrently mapped meltwater was concentrated in western and southwestern sectors and along central flow‐aligned zones. The fracture maps showed broadly similar regional zones. The 2014 and 2025 seasonal indices had higher relative values in the western and southwestern sectors. The multi‐year recurrence–fracture comparison showed a similar regional concentration. Adding maximum retrieved depth from seasons ending in 2014–2025 further localised the highest relative multi‐year index values in these sectors. The southeastern sector contained extensive mapped fractures with comparatively limited hydrological co‐location. These results identify regional concentrations of recurrently mapped meltwater, greater retrieved depth and mapped fractures.

title: Expansion of North Atlantic Deep Water during Northern Hemisphere Glaciation
abstract: Abstract Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a major driver of the Earth’s climate, moving heat from the Southern Hemisphere to the Northern Hemisphere. Neither foraminiferal carbon isotope records nor modelling studies agree on the spatial extent of North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW), the northern deep limb of the AMOC, over the intensification of Northern Hemisphere Glaciation (iNHG, ~2.73 million years ago). Here we present high-resolution neodymium isotope (ε Nd ) records from a depth transect in the equatorial Atlantic over the iNHG. We find a persistent latitudinal and depth gradient in neodymium isotope values in the deep Atlantic during the Late Pliocene, absent in the Early Pleistocene, indicating an expansion of NADW extent over the iNHG. In contrast, our reconstruction suggests very little glacial-interglacial variability in NADW extent during both the Late Pliocene and Early Pleistocene. These results suggest deep-water circulation was substantially different during a warm climate state, with implications for the role of NADW formation during major climate transitions and its future stability.

title: An age calculator for high-latitude Quaternary foraminifera using amino acid racemization
abstract: Dating deep-sea cores from polar regions is challenging because sedimentation rates can be variable and oxygen-isotope stratigraphy can be ineffective, making amino acid racemization an important alternative. We calibrated the rate of racemization in Neogloboquadrina pachyderma , the dominant high-latitude planktic foraminifer, using 140 independently dated samples from 21 Arctic, Nordic Seas, North Atlantic, and Southern Ocean sites spanning 2 ka to 1.4 Ma. Racemization rates among these ocean basins differ less than among individual sites. Ages are based on aspartic acid, a more precise chronometer than glutamic acid, which, however, provides an independent check on the analysis. A publicly available age calculator returns formal uncertainty intervals incorporating calibration and measurement errors. Ages carry a realistic uncertainty of roughly ± 32% (66% level), insufficient to assign a sample to a specific Marine Isotope Stage but still useful for many polar marine sediment cores. A single age picks correctly between two candidate ages 90% of the time when they differ by a factor of 2.3 (e.g., 100 versus 230 ka). An independently dated horizon in the same core can reduce the uncertainty to ± 28%. Because comparisons are more precise than absolute ages, amino acid geochronology is best applied as a down-core series.

title: An accurate present-day model of the Antarctic ice sheet is necessary but insufficient for an accurate projection of its future evolution
abstract: Computer models of the Antarctic ice sheet can project how much it will melt in response to climate change. That depends on the properties of the rock and the water beneath the ice, about which we know very little. That means the amount of sea-level in the future is very uncertain. Techniques to reduce that uncertainty do not always work as well as expected. We must get actual measurements of the bottom of the ice to improve our understanding of the ice sheet, and our knowledge of its future.
authors: Roderik S. W. van de Wal

title: Isotope-based age scale with multi-month precision for the SE-Dome II ice core from Southeast Greenland over the past 150 years
abstract: We developed a new 150-year age scale for an ice core from southeast Greenland by matching its oxygen-isotope variations with climate-model simulations. The record resolves changes over several months and shows that snowfall remained nearly evenly distributed through the seasons from 1871 to 2020. This stability suggests that the regional balance of atmospheric circulation and moisture transport changed little at this site despite recent Arctic warming.

title: Sub-daily multi-pass AMSR2 passive microwave response to the 2012 extreme melt event in northwestern Greenland
abstract: The unprecedented Greenland Ice Sheet melt in summer 2012 provides a natural experiment to evaluate how spaceborne passive microwave brightness temperature ( T B ) responds to extreme melt on diurnal timescales. We analyzed multi-frequency AMSR2 T B from GCOM–W over a northwestern Greenland site (SIGMA–A) and compared the radiometric evolution with in situ snow temperatures and surface energy balance terms derived from automated weather station meteorology. From early to mid-July 2012, T B showed coherent, frequency- and polarization-dependent transitions through the major melt event, including a pronounced shift in diurnal behavior. Outside the melt peak, high-frequency T B (36.5 and 89.0 GHz) exhibited clear day–night contrast, whereas during the extreme melt period T B remained elevated with a strongly damped diurnal range, consistent with sustained nighttime wetness. At 89.0 GHz, T B increases coincided with persistently positive surface energy input dominated by enhanced downward longwave radiation and peak cloud occurrence inferred from Aqua/MODIS and all-sky imagery, supporting a cloud-linked high-frequency enhancement. In contrast, low-frequency T B (6.9–10.7 GHz) decreased, most strongly in H-pol, consistent with melt-driven reductions in effective emissivity associated with wet–dry dielectric contrasts. Most notably, the 6.9–7.3 GHz difference revealed a distinct polarization-dependent post-melt transition: after the melt peak, Δ T B, H showed increased variability and occasional positive values, whereas Δ T B, V remained nearly unchanged at negative values. This behavior indicates that the 6.9–7.3 GHz H-pol pair is sensitive not only to melt-driven changes in low-frequency emission, but also to refreezing-modified near-surface stratigraphy. These results demonstrate that multi-frequency microwave radiometry can resolve rapid snow–firn transitions during extreme melt and identify the 6.9–7.3 GHz H-pol difference as a compact diagnostic that complements conventional melt monitoring by capturing post-melt near-surface structural evolution.

title: Evaluation of reanalysis datasets for studying high-elevation meteorological conditions in the Langtang Catchment, Nepal
abstract: Climate reanalysis datasets are widely used in hydro-meteorological and cryospheric research across High Mountain Asia (HMA), where in situ observations are scarce. Here, we evaluate ERA5L, High Asian Refined Analysis (HARv2), Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis for Research and Applications (MERRA2), and Climatologies at High Resolution for the Earth’s Land Surface Areas (CHELSA) against near-surface meteorological observations between 3,865 and 5,350 m a.s.l., in the upper Langtang Catchment, Nepal, using statistical metrics and Taylor Skill Score ( TSS ). We further assess their suitability for glacier surface energy balance (SEB) and mass balance modelling. No reanalysis product consistently outperforms the others; rather, their performance varies by meteorological variable, site, surface conditions, and timescale, with generally better performance at glacier sites, likely because their relatively homogeneous surface conditions are more readily represented by reanalysis products. Near-surface air temperature ( T 2m ) and humidity (specific: q and relative: RH ) are well reproduced ( TSS > 0.77) across products, although cold temperature and both dry and moist humidity biases are pervasive across sites. Wind speed ( u ) is poorly represented across products, sites, and timescales, reflecting their limited ability to resolve boundary layer processes and local katabatic and anabatic flows. Precipitation also exhibits large discrepancies, with ERA5L and HARv2 overestimating precipitation totals by ∼89–232% and MERRA2 and CHELSA underestimating by 30%–60%. They also generate frequent wet days and early-afternoon convective rainfall, in contrast to observed late-afternoon and nocturnal-to-early morning maxima. Hourly and daily SEB simulations at the Yala-on-Glacier site driven by reanalysis forcings yield statistically significant surface melt relative to reference estimates driven by in situ datasets; however, substantial differences in magnitude exist among products. ERA5L and HARv2 exhibit relatively small errors, largely due to compensating errors between radiative and turbulent fluxes, whereas MERRA2 and CHELSA show larger melt discrepancies due to their large radiative flux errors and underestimated precipitation that affects the surface albedo. Overall, our results underscore both the usefulness and limitations of reanalysis products for cryospheric applications in complex mountainous catchments and emphasize the need for assimilation of high-elevation observations in reanalysis products, alongside improved downscaling approaches, to better resolve local-scale atmospheric processes.

title: Drivers of reduced permafrost cooling efficacy of equatorial stratospheric aerosol injection in the Eastern Arctic compared to a moderate emission pathway
abstract: The Arctic is warming faster than the rest of the world, causing permafrost – frozen ground – to thaw and release gases that accelerate climate change. Because emissions are not falling quickly enough, ways to cool the planet by reflecting sunlight back to space are being explored. Using climate model experiments, we study how this could affect permafrost. We find it could slow overall loss later this century, but shift thaw patterns, reducing it in some regions while increasing it in others.

title: A valley system investigation of Holocene coastal change and Irish Sea palaeogeography in Cardigan Bay, Wales, UK
abstract: Of the three substantial areas of postglacial aerial exposure on the Irish Sea shelf (Liverpool Bay, Cardigan Bay and the Bristol Channel), Cardigan Bay is the largest and the one about which we know the least. This article provides the first empirical sea level data for Cardigan Bay since the 1980s. It examines the proposition that the valleys of north Cardigan Bay were subject to a long period of marine influence that is not modelled in current palaeogeographical reconstructions. Detailed lithostratigraphic investigations traced the extent of Early to Mid‐Holocene marine influence in the Dysynni valley. Multiple microfossil proxies were used to calculate sea level data points. Two sea level index points from a back‐barrier marsh indicated relative sea level rise from −5.55 to −3.13 mOD between 7790–7630 and 6399–6296 cal. a BP. Freshwater/terrestrial limiting points from 7 km inland bracketed a period of marine influence between 9889–9545 and 4783–4416 cal. a BP. Pollen recorded a transition from saltmarsh, fen and reed‐swamp environments to alder carr and then birch woodland. The results were combined with existing lithostratigraphic and biostratigraphic data to show that the overdeepened glacial valleys of north Cardigan Bay were subject to marine influence from before 12 000 cal. a BP, with different palaeogeographical histories dependent on their depths and rates of postglacial sedimentation.

title: Spatial Shift in Southern Ocean Seasonal Ice Zone Production Trends
abstract: In recent decades, satellite observations have reported a marked increase in primary production across the Seasonal Ice Zone (SIZ) of the Southern Ocean, indicating enhanced ecosystem activity and a potential rise in biological carbon storage. However, the spatial coherence and temporal stability of these trends remain poorly constrained. Here, using satellite observations and model-based data from 1998/99 to 2023/24, we detect two successive regime shifts in austral summer SIZ primary production. The first, around 2007/08, marks a transition from a dipole—characterized by declining production in the Weddell Sea and increasing production in the Amundsen Sea—to a basin-wide increase across the SIZ. The second, around 2014/15, represents an intensification of this basin-wide pattern under accelerated sea-ice loss. Mechanistically, the initial 2007/08 structural shift is likely triggered by the reversal of the Southern Annular Mode (SAM), which restructured regional sea-ice distribution via rapid Ekman-driven atmospheric forcing. For the post-2007/08 period, sea-ice redistribution fundamentally altered light penetration, while wind-driven mixed-layer shoaling further enhanced light availability, promoting a widespread rebound in primary production. In contrast, the slow response to persistent SAM forcing—via enhanced Circumpolar Deep Water upwelling—progressively decreased sea-ice concentration, reaching a critical tipping point around 2014/15 that accelerated the basin-wide sea-ice decline. For the post-2014/15 period, the accelerated sea-ice loss directly reduced surface albedo and introduced substantial meltwater, which further shoaled the mixed layer, collectively driving a stronger productivity increase. These results have implications for projecting future changes in regional primary production and assessing the broader impacts on the Southern Ocean's biological carbon pump.

title: Snow Phenology over Antarctic Sea Ice and Its Lagged Relationship with Sea Ice Thickness
journal: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
abstract: Snow over Antarctic sea ice influences surface energy exchange, sea-ice growth, and surface mass balance, yet its seasonal evolution remains poorly understood due to sparse observations and uncertainties among retrieval methods. The timing of Antarctic sea-ice transitions has also exhibited substantial regional variability, raising the need to understand how snow phenology evolves with sea-ice conditions. Here, monthly snow-depth reconstructions from three deep-learning frameworks, including a convolutional neural network (CNN), the Kolmogorov–Arnold network (KAN), and multilayer perceptron (MLP), are used to characterize Antarctic snow phenology, including snow-onset month, snow-melt month, snow-season length, and annual maximum snow depth. Spatial trends of phenological metrics are quantified, and lagged relationships between snow depth and sea-ice thickness (SIT) are examined across 0–5 month lags. All three reconstruction frameworks reproduce the dominant seasonal cycle of Antarctic snow depth, characterized by reduced accumulation during austral summer and enhanced accumulation during winter and spring. The derived phenological metrics exhibit pronounced regional variability, with model differences most evident in snow-melt timing and snow-season length. Trend patterns reveal spatially heterogeneous changes rather than a uniform circumpolar response. Correlations between monthly snow-depth and SIT anomalies are strongest at short lags and decrease with increasing temporal offsets, showing that their monthly departures are most closely aligned over short intervals. The spread among reconstructions highlights the influence of model-dependent uncertainty on derived snow-phenology indicators and emphasizes the importance of multi-model assessments for interpreting Antarctic snow–ice coupling.

title: A record of polyphase Middle Pleistocene glaciation in the Sudetic Foreland, SW Poland
abstract: The Sudetic Foreland of Central Europe preserves an important sedimentary archive for reconstructing Pleistocene dynamics of the Scandinavian Ice Sheet, although the timing and character of pre-Saalian glaciations remain poorly constrained. This study presents an integrated sedimentological, structural, petrographic, and geochronological investigation of glaciogenic deposits exposed at the Jaźwina gravel pit. Two litho-petrographically distinct till units (T1 and T2) record changes in sediment provenance linked to the South Polish Complex (Elsterian1/2; MIS12/16). Glaciotectonic mesostructures indicate deformation under WNW–ESE-directed compression, interpreted as the combined effect of ice loading and reactivation of the Sudetic Marginal Fault. 10 Be– 26 Al burial dating of Fennoscandian erratics from the lower T1 till constrains its maximum depositional age to 620 ± 480 ka. Macrofossil wood remains (Quercus sp., Abies sp.) beneath the glacial succession are interpreted as redeposited from Early Pleistocene fluvial sediments. The combination of deformed tills, variable provenance signatures, and overprinted ice-flow indicators supports a polyphase glacial history involving thrust stacking of Middle Pleistocene deposits and subsequent tectonically driven denudation of the uppermost MIS 6 (Uciechów) till. These findings provide the first direct cosmogenic-nuclide age constraints for Middle Pleistocene tills and underscore the value of site-specific studies for resolving pre-Saalian glacial chronologies in Central Europe.

title: Coupled Ocean–Atmosphere Processes Associated with Realistically Sized Weddell Sea Polynyas in CMIP6 Models
abstract: Abstract The mechanisms of the Weddell Sea Polynya have been frequently discussed in the literature since the first and largest observed opening in the 1970s, with smaller Maud Rise Polynyas opening in more recent years. Here we assess both the oceanic and atmospheric preconditioning and response associated with polynya events, using Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) Pre-industrial Control models. Here, we focus on polynyas with realistic size and location (i.e., comparable to the 1970s events). Only two models in the CMIP6 suite produce such realistic polynyas in large numbers, ACCESS-ESM1.5 and MPI-ESM1-2-HR. Their oceanic and atmospheric preconditioning and atmospheric response are explored using a composite analysis. We find that weakened stratification sets the oceanic preconditioning, while the onset of polynya years is associated with the occurrence of large-scale atmospheric internal variability, including a ZW3-like pressure and wind pattern. Both modes emerge from internal atmospheric variability, suggesting that the first occurrence in a series of polynya years is stochastic in nature. Once the polynya opens, two-way air-sea feedbacks deepen the sea level pressure anomalies, enabling multi-year polynya events. Through this, the stratification returns to a base level, the ocean state recharges, and the cycle repeats. These results advance understanding of Weddell Sea Polynya formation and highlight the importance of coupled ocean–atmosphere feedbacks in the Southern Ocean.

title: Bioclimatic and habitat signals in Pleistocene fluvial microvertebrate assemblages from the Middle Dnipro region, Ukraine
abstract: Fluvial microvertebrate assemblages are important but underexplored archives for reconstructing Quaternary environments, particularly in regions lacking karstic and cave deposits. We analyse late Middle and early Late Pleistocene small‐vertebrate assemblages from the Middle Dnipro region, Ukraine, to compare two interpretative frameworks: habitat‐weighting analysis and bioclimatic spectra. The studied assemblages span multiple Marine Isotope Stages (MIS 11 to MIS 5) and derive exclusively from alluvial contexts characterised by taphonomic overprinting and time‐averaging. Using principal component analysis, we compare the environmental signals extracted by both methods across different taxonomic datasets. In both approaches, the dominant source of variation reflects changes in ecological evenness, expressed as shifts in the relative importance of steppe, tundra–steppe and high‐latitude taxa. The most even assemblages correspond to cold‐stage conditions and are characterised by arctic and boreal elements, whereas low‐evenness assemblages are dominated by core tundra–steppe taxa. Habitat spectra additionally capture geomorphological influences related to river‐valley dynamics, resulting in a diffuse climatic signal. In contrast, bioclimatic spectra more directly resolve glacial–interglacial climatic gradients and show greater robustness to incomplete faunal lists and taphonomic biases. Our results demonstrate that bioclimatic spectra provide a clearer palaeoclimatic signal than habitat‐based approaches for fluvial microvertebrate assemblages. This method is therefore particularly well suited to Quaternary environmental reconstruction in lowland river systems affected by taphonomic and sedimentary filtering.

title: Last glacial North Pacific oxygenation due to North Atlantic circulation changes
abstract: Nature Geoscience, Published online: 23 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02122-x Transient weakening of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation during the last glacial period may have led to a contraction of oxygen minimum zones in the North Pacific, according to benthic foraminifera proxy records and Earth system simulations.

title: Using a Gaussian process emulator to approximate short-term climate response patterns to greenhouse gas and aerosol forcings
abstract: We present a fast machine learning emulator that predicts how Earth's surface temperature reacts within the first five years to changes in greenhouse gases and aerosol pollutants. It is trained on carefully designed simulations from a complex climate model, but can be run much faster. Our emulator can be used to show where the climate is most sensitive to different emissions and can help explore many possible future paths, making it easier to assess the climate effects of policy choices.

title: An antiplane shear model for evaluating shear-margin stability (Ortholine v1.0)
abstract: The widths of glaciers and ice streams can change over time, which strongly affects how much ice is lost to the ocean. Many existing models of sea-level rise neglect these width changes, but they are commonly observed and important. This paper presents a new, simple model that helps identify which physical factors govern width changes at different field sites. The model is explained step by step and tested using an Antarctic ice stream as an example.

title: A small ensemble of bias-adjusted CMIP6 climate simulations over North America extending to 2300
abstract: Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) Even if many sectors would benefit from scientific evidence on the long-term consequences of current policy choices, most climate projections end in 2100. This paper describes a collection of bias-adjusted climate simulations extending to 2300. It includes few Earth System Models, most of them driven by scenarios at the very low or very high end of the range of plausible futures. The composition of the ensemble makes it difficult to deliver climate services supporting climate risk assessments.

title: Exchange between ocean and Greenland fjords regulated by recirculating meltwater in glacial troughs
abstract: Nature Geoscience, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02147-2 The recirculation of glacial meltwater within a deep Greenland fjord inhibits the inflow of relatively warm ocean water, slowing further glacial melt, according to hydrographic observations and numerical modelling.

title: Post-depositional geochemical transformations of aerosol impurities in EPICA Dome C ice core: dissolution, mineral neoformation, and immobilization revealed by CFA-sp-ICP-TOFMS
abstract: Deep ice cores preserve records of past climate, but chemical reactions inside the ice can blur these signals over time. To find out how, we studied millions of dust particles in a deep Antarctic ice core. We found that, over long timescales, dust dissolves and reforms into new minerals within tiny pockets of liquid, trapping chemical elements. Warm temperatures speed up this process. Accounting for it helps scientists interpret ancient climate records from deep ice more reliably.

title: Attribution of climate extremes with global temperature regressions: accounting for uncertainty from internal variability
abstract: Attribution of climate change to anthropogenic forcing is an important goal in climate science. Regression of local conditions on global temperatures is a popular statistical approach, but whether the uncertainty derived from observations alone can reflect the range of outcomes possible due to internal variability remains unclear. Here, we use large ensembles from three climate models as an idealized testbed to quantify the role of internal variability for such attribution of climate extremes with single climate realisations. Internal variability generates large uncertainty in the linear-regression slope between global temperatures and regional temperature extremes, exceeding 40% of the ensemble mean slope across 50, 38, and 9% of the global surface area in the MIROC6, MPI-ESM1-2-LR and CanESM5 models respectively. Nevertheless, we show that these uncertainties can be accurately inferred from individual ensemble members using a block-bootstrap procedure - offering potential for a robust application to observations. Block-bootstrapping also accurately captures the absolute uncertainty for precipitation extremes, despite a substantially smaller signal-to-noise ratio which leads to underestimated and overly noisy estimates of relative uncertainty at present-day warming levels. This work provides a basis for the attribution of climate extremes from observations which can robustly capture the uncertainty associated with internal climate variability.

title: Estimating the impact of ice-sheet surface height and ice-divide variability on ice-core based climate reconstructions
abstract: Ice drilled from deep inside Antarctica reveals how climate changed over hundreds of thousands of years. However, the ice sheet itself rises and sinks over time, which can distort temperatures read from the ice. Using three computer simulations covering the last two million years, we show that drilling sites rose and sank by up to 240 metres and their summits shifted by up to 120 kilometres, and we estimate how this biases climate records, including potential for the oldest ice.

title: Alternate states and intermingledness in complex high-dimensional systems
abstract: by George Datseris, Johannes Lohmann, Oisín Hamilton, Jacob Haqq-Misra Many natural systems posses, and can transition between, multiple alternative states. For example, a climate “tipping element” is a climate component that can transition to an alternative steady state due to an external perturbation such as global warming. Despite the potential impact, existence of alternate states in realistic, complex simulations (e.g., climate models) remain poorly understood. Arguably a reason for this is the lack of applicable methodology that explicitly targets finite yet high-dimensional datasets. In this work we utilize recent progress in computational nonlinear dynamics to formulate a workflow that analyses potentially multi-state simulation data and decides algorithmically what are the alternate states contained within, if any are clearly distinguishable. The framework undergoes an optimization routine that showcases which observables in the data best differentiate the alternate states, and which ones do not differentiate at all, which could be used to guide monitoring and early-warning for multistable components in climate or ecosystems. Finally, once the alternate states have been found, we define an indicator called “intermingledness”. It quantifies differences and similarities between alternate states, as well as for their basins of attraction (if applicable), across various diagnostic variables. We analyse and present results using three diverse climate datasets: Atlantic ocean circulation, atmospheric midlatitude flow, and habitability of exoplanets. The method is not exclusive to climatic data, but applicable to a variety of cases characterised by high dimensional data and presence of alternate states, including complex networks such as power grids or biological networks. We also provide easy-to-use open source code for applying the workflow to new data.

title: Future meltwater dynamics and water balance components under climate warming and land use change in a cryosphere-dominated basin of the Tibetan plateau
Beyond Resolution: Inference-Time Parameterized Temporal Consistency in Generative Regional Climate Downscaling
abstract: arXiv:2611.27641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GCM-to-RCM downscaling emulation is dominated by generative diffusion models, but most existing work evaluates skill only per timestep, treating each field as an independent snapshot. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. We introduce a noise-conditioned teacher-forcing training scheme conditioning a diffusion U-Net downscaling model on a noised previous high-resolution state, so the trained model interpolates continuously between autoregressive (AR) and per-timestep independent (PTI) sampling via one noise parameter. We apply the scheme to an hourly, European-domain historical simulation downscaling AWI-CM1 (1$^\circ$) with ICON (0.11$^\circ$, regridded to 0.25$^\circ$) for precipitation and 2-meter temperature. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. These results show that in diffusion downscaling temporal consistency can be achieved architecture-agnostically and offered as a controllable, not fixed, inference choice.

title: Glacier Albedo Variability During Transportation Infrastructure Construction: A Case Study of the Tianshan Shengli Tunnel
abstract: Glacier surface albedo influences melt and may respond to climatic variability, changing surface conditions, and particulate emissions from nearby infrastructure. This study examined albedo variability across 434 glaciers near the Tianshan Shengli Tunnel during 2018–2024 using MODIS MOD10A1, Landsat 8/9 observations, ERA5 winds, and excavation records. Mean albedo during 2020–2024 was lower than during 2018–2019 by 0.025 for MODIS and 0.032 for Landsat. A distinct MODIS pixel-level quality-screening comparison applying an 80% daily valid-area coverage threshold yielded a descriptive difference of −0.0278. In the matched 357-glacier August–September sample, trends were −0.00597 yr−1 for the original masks and −0.00615 yr−1 after 60 m inward buffering; both 95% confidence intervals included zero. Cross-sensor observations covaried strongly (r = 0.867), although the bias of −0.073 and RMSE of 0.086 indicated substantial disagreement in magnitude. The climate-adjusted MODIS post-2020 coefficient was non-significant (−0.0190; p = 0.287), while the Landsat coefficient changed sign with trend specification. Across six excavation intervals, the construction-activity proxy showed a non-significant association with albedo anomalies (Spearman ρ = −0.543; exact p = 0.297), with direction sensitive to the reference baseline. Seasonal wind alignment described regional directional relationships but did not establish particle transport or deposition. The observations document lower later-period albedo and a negative interior-mask trend tendency without isolating a construction contribution. These findings support continuous dust control during emission-generating activities and coordinated glacier, meteorological, and deposition monitoring.

title: Distinguishing dynamic and thermal effects of the Tibetan Plateau on the Asian dust cycle using regional climate modeling
abstract: The Tibetan Plateau (TP) has profound influence on the Asian dust cycle through dynamic and thermal effects, yet quantification of the impacts of these effects remains inadequate. This study employed the Regional Climate Model (RegCM4) to systematically quantify the impacts of the two effects of the TP on dust cycle across six major Asian deserts through numerical experiments. The simulated results revealed that the dynamic effect suppresses springtime dust emission in the Taklimakan Desert by more than 500 mg m −2 day −1 but enhances that considerably (by almost 300–500 mg m −2 day −1) over the Loess Plateau. The thermal effect intensifies summer dust activity in the Thar Desert (by 500 mg m −2 day −1) and the Qaidam Basin, and is closely linked to strong convection and monsoon flows. The dust loading of East Asia peaks in spring under the dominance of the dynamic effect of the TP, while that in South Asia peaks in summer, driven primarily by the thermal effect of the TP. The dust deposition patterns indicate that the dynamic effect inhibits dust accumulation in the Taklimakan Desert, but promotes deposition on the Loess Plateau. The thermal effect enhances dust deposition through monsoon-related changes in soil moisture. The dynamic effect alters near-surface winds via topographic channeling and jet stream bifurcation, while the thermal effect modulates boundary layer stability and the large-scale circulations. This quantitative study elucidated how the dual forcings of the TP dynamically shape the patterns of the Asian dust cycle, providing critical constraints for Earth System Models.

title: Enabling joint chemical and meteorological data assimilation with an atmospheric foundation model
abstract: arXiv:2611.24020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The hydroxyl radical (OH) is the main oxidant in the troposphere and accounts for 88% of the methane sink, yet its abundance and trends remain poorly constrained. Satellites observe many of the chemical and meteorological drivers of OH, but assimilating both requires a model that represents chemistry and meteorology together. Existing chemistry-climate models are too expensive for joint data assimilation. Here, we present AuroraChem, a fine-tuned version of the Aurora atmospheric foundation model that jointly simulates meteorology and the GEOS-Chem chemical fields needed to constrain OH. A one-year AuroraChem rollout takes 12 minutes on one GPU. Free rollouts remain stable for one year but do not fully capture seasonal cycles. Using idealized data assimilation, we find that chemical observations can constrain the meteorological state and meteorological observations can constrain the chemical state. Inserting only the chemical fields raises the annual mean spatial correlation of 500 hPa temperature from 0.89 to 0.92 and recovers the moisture and circulation pattern of the Indian summer monsoon. Inserting only the meteorological fields raises the 500 hPa OH correlation from 0.89 to 0.93, close to the 0.94 from inserting the chemical fields themselves, and recovers the OH seasonal cycle. Inserting only NO2 columns sampled at TROPOMI pixels gives an OH correlation of 0.93. These relationships likely reflect learned covariances rather than physical coupling, and covariances are what data assimilation uses to let an observation of one variable update the others. AuroraChem therefore provides a new pathway to joint chemical and meteorological data assimilation.

title: MAIC-2 v2.3: A Fortran program for simulating the surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation of the planet Mars
abstract: arXiv:2611.23643v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Mars Atmosphere-Ice Coupler MAIC-2 is a computationally efficient, zonally-averaged model designed to simulate Martian surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation over timescales of 10^5 to 10^7 years. While sophisticated General Circulation Models (GCMs) provide high-resolution simulations of the Martian atmosphere, their high computational cost makes them largely unsuitable for studies covering millions of years of orbital evolution. MAIC-2 addresses this gap by utilizing physically-based, zonally-averaged parameterizations, including a Local Insolation Temperature (LIT) scheme and a mass balance engine driven by free-convection and instantaneous mixing physics. Version 2.3 introduces a fully modularized Fortran architecture that improves maintainability and ensures that the software remains entirely self-contained, requiring no external numerical libraries or specialized data formats for execution. Demonstrated through a 20-million-year transient simulation, the model successfully reproduces the primary characteristics of the Martian polar layered deposits. MAIC-2 provides the planetary science community with a versatile, open-source tool for investigating the long-term climatic impacts of orbital variations on the Martian surface.

title: Global Holocene Stalagmite Growth Rates and Their Climatic Associations
abstract: Stalagmite growth rates record cave carbonate deposition and environmental change, but their climatic associations remain insufficiently tested at the global Holocene scale. We compiled 218 stalagmites from 139 caves in SISALv3, calculated mean Holocene growth rates, and matched their growth intervals to gridded paleoclimate variables. Spearman rank correlations, partial least-squares regression, and XGBoost classification were used to assess climatic associations. Growth rates ranged from 0.003 to 1.75 mm yr−1, with 75% of samples below 0.1248 mm yr−1. Annual precipitation showed a weak positive correlation with growth rate (ρ = 0.161), whereas wettest-quarter precipitation, precipitation seasonality, precipitation concentration, and wet-season precipitation ratio showed stronger correlations with growth rate (ρ = 0.288–0.306). Temperature associations were more consistent: mean annual, coldest-quarter, and wettest-quarter temperatures were positively correlated with growth rate (ρ = 0.356–0.422), while temperature seasonality was negatively correlated (ρ = −0.328). An XGBoost model using five climate variables achieved 69.32% accuracy in two-fold cross-validation. These results indicate that climate captures part of the spatial variability in stalagmite growth. Growth rates reflect the combined effects of effective recharge, thermal conditions, karst hydrology, and cave depositional environments, providing a global reference for interpreting Holocene stalagmite records.

title: Observationally-constrained CMIP6 projections of a snow-free Northern Hemisphere
abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79797-8 This study presents a monthly emergent constraint based on observed warming that reduces CMIP6 inter-model variance and refines snow-free projections: Arctic summers become snow-free by 2040 s under SSP5-8.5, while snow disappearance is delayed by 7–34 years under SSP1-2.6 in vulnerable regions and months.

title: Boron isotopes in fluvial palaeochannels reveal catchment weathering and climate variability over the last glacial–interglacial cycle
abstract: Boron (B) isotopes in fluvial clay fractions can provide information about catchment weathering and vegetation–soil interactions during past environmental change. We investigate clay- and sand-fraction B isotope compositions, clay B/Al ratios, mineralogy and neodymium isotopes from 14 sites across four Murrumbidgee River palaeochannel systems in southeastern Australia, spanning the last glacial–interglacial cycle. Sampling position, mineralogical assemblages and geochemical observations are combined to assess potential post-depositional overprinting. Several shallow or exposed samples have elevated δ 11 B, consistent with interaction with isotopically heavy soil or pore waters. In the screened dataset, clay–sand isotope offsets (Δ 11 Bclay–sand) are relatively low in Yanco and Gum Creek sediments and more positive in Kerarbury, Coleambally and recent deposits. Overlapping εNd compositions provide no clear evidence for a systematic provenance shift among systems. The boron isotope contrasts, considered alongside regional vegetation records and clay mineralogy, suggest changes in the influence of biologically modified soil solutions on catchment weathering products. More positive offsets are consistent with greater vegetation-mediated B cycling, whereas lower offsets in the younger systems may reflect reduced biological processing, increased contributions from deeper regolith, or both. Published palaeohydrological evidence places these younger deposits within periods of enhanced fluvial activity, suggesting that greater water and sediment delivery coexisted with a reduced biological imprint on exported clays. The results demonstrate the potential of boron isotopes to complement fluvial and vegetation archives by tracing changes in catchment weathering regime, while emphasising the importance of assessing post-depositional preservation.

title: Long-term observations of hydrography, phytoplankton pigments, and suspended particles in Potter Cove (Antarctica), 1991–2025
abstract: Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) Antarctica is changing, but long-term coastal observations remain rare. This study brings together more than 30 years of data from Potter Cove, Antarctica, including seawater temperature, salt content, microscopic plant pigments, and suspended particles. By combining thousands of observations collected across seasons, this dataset provides a unique resource for understanding environmental change and ecosystem responses, aiding to understand how Antarctic coastal waters may change in the future.

title: Warming Trends on the Hurd Peninsula of Livingston Island, Antarctica, Between 2000 and 2024, and Improvements in the Estimation of Air Temperature Using C6.1 MODIS LST Data
abstract: Analysing the spatial and temporal variability of near-surface air temperature (Ta) is essential for assessing climate change, particularly in polar regions such as the maritime Antarctic, where observational studies remain comparatively scarce. In areas with sparse meteorological networks, satellite observations provide a valuable means of extending station-based analyses and generating spatially distributed Ta maps. This study analyses updated Ta records from six meteorological stations on the Hurd Peninsula, Livingston Island, for 2000–2024, with particular attention to temperature changes since 2016, and evaluates Ta estimation models based on MODIS Terra daytime LST Collection 6.1 data. The analysis of the Ta time series showed significant warming over the complete 2000–2024 period, with trends ranging from 0.53 to 1.27 °C decade−1, and a clear shift towards warming after 2016. While the 2000–2015 period showed spatially contrasting trends, including cooling at JCI, positive trends were observed at all analysed stations during 2016–2024, ranging from 0.40 to 1.33 °C decade−1 and highlighting substantial local variability across the Hurd Peninsula. The global Ta model, developed using data from all six stations and based on MODIS Terra daytime LST and spatiotemporal variables, achieved a performance comparable to that obtained with Collection 6, with R2 = 0.77 and a cross-validated RMSE of 2.23 °C. The results also showed that rigorous filtering of the MODIS LST observations is essential: retaining only good-quality data and excluding observations with |view angle| > 45° substantially reduced dispersion in the Ta–LST relationship and removed unrealistically low LST values. The introduction of this view-angle threshold represents a new filtering step with respect to our previous studies.

title: Modelling the effects of proglacial lake filling and drainage on lake-terminating glacier dynamics
abstract: Ice sheet/glacier retreat is driving expansion of glacial lakes impounded at the ice margin. Using an ice sheet model, we find that lake filling and drainage causes systematic changes to glacier thickness, velocity and mass loss. Rising lake levels dramatically increase mass loss as the ice margin becomes buoyant, while rapid lake drainage can drive crevassing and destabilise the margin. Steady lake drainage, in contrast, has a stabilising effect, and may mitigate mass loss and flood hazards.

title: Milanković’s Theory of Ice Ages and Serbian Loess
abstract: The text deals with Milanković’s Mathematical–Astronomical Theory of Ice Ages and its connection with Serbian loess. Here it is recalled, put into the context of the people who collaborated with Milanković during his work (W. Köppen, A. Wegener, V. Mišković, W. Jardetzky, D. Mitrinović, and S. Fempl), and it points to its 50th anniversary of verification in the journal Science. Then, the Theory is compared with magnetic susceptibility (MS) profiles of two Serbian loess–paleosol sequences (Mošorin and Stari Slankamen) by (i) showing side-by-side the Milanković’s Insolation Curves and the MS Curves over the last 600,000 years and (ii) discussing the relation of the MS spectral components and the orbital (eccentricity, obliquity, and precession) and terrestrial (solar constant and albedo) forcing of Milankovic’sTheory. In addition to the similarities between Milanković’s Insolation Curves and the MS Curves, there are discrepancies, the causes of which are analyzed in detail. The text ends with a biographical section on Milanković’s voyages down the Danube and the StariSlankamen profile, where in the layers of loess there are visual traces of the change in glacial (Ice Ages), cold intervals and interglacial (Inter Ice Ages), warm intervals in the geological history of the Earth. These traces match relatively well with Milanković’s Insolation Curves, which he could not have known during his many passes. In the conclusion, suggestions are given on how to reduce the discrepancies between Milanković’s Insolation Curves and the MS Curves and thereby improve paleoclimatological research.

title: Disentangling positional change from intensity in the palaeoclimate reconstruction of circulation patterns
abstract: Abstract Under ongoing anthropogenic climate change, the impacts of forcing on climate circulation patterns, such as ocean currents and wind belts, are an area of particular scientific interest. Due to the complexity of the system, these subsystem patterns can exhibit multi-dimensional variability such as strength change or feature migration. However, conventional proxy-based reconstructions risk conflating positional shifts with intensity changes, thereby obscuring the true mode of past variability and potentially impeding the accuracy of hindcasts and predictions. Here, we present this issue and discuss three subsystems where previous work has attempted to disentangle spatial and magnitudinal change, namely the Gulf Stream, Intertropical Convergence Zone, and Southern Hemisphere westerly winds. Our analysis of deployed methodologies finds that studies principally employ spatial networks and dimension-specific proxies to separate these compounding effects. We emphasise the importance of incorporating this interpretation challenge into future study design and highlight the need for new disentanglement methods. This review synthesises existing disentanglement approaches, provides a concise conceptual framing, and offers practical recommendations for study design.

Diagnosing the Roles of Large-Scale Circulation in Tropical Precipitation Biases in CESM2 Using Nudging Technique
abstract: Persistent tropical precipitation biases in general circulation models can arise from errors in both the large-scale environment and the subgrid-scale processes that produce precipitation, making their respective contributions difficult to isolate. Here, we evaluate precipitation in the Community Earth System Model version 2.2.2 (CESM2) using a revised nudging framework that constrains horizontal winds, specific humidity, and/or temperature toward reanalysis. Constraining horizontal winds substantially reduces climatological precipitation biases across the tropical Pacific, including dry biases over the western Pacific warm pool and northern Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) and wet biases in the subtropics. Importantly, replacing the largescale circulation with reanalysis also shifts precipitation from overly frequent light rainfall toward heavier intensities, despite no modifications to the model’s moist physics parameterizations. This improvement is closely associated with reorganized moisture transport and more frequent strong moisture convergence events, even in regions where the climatological humidity does not increase. Further constraining specific humidity or temperature provides no systematic additional improvement, highlighting the central role of circulation in setting the environment to which moist physics parameterizations respond. However, regional biases remain, particularly an underestimation of heavy precipitation, even though model’s lower troposphere remains closer to saturation than in reanalysis during substantial precipitation events. Together, the substantial shift from overly frequent light rainfall toward heavier intensities under circulation constraint indicates that errors in the large-scale environment contribute importantly to precipitation biases in CESM2, while the remaining discrepancies likely also reflect limitations in the moist physics parameterizations.

title: The importance of deep time from Hutton to Earth system science
